question: A class implements an interface method but declares it without `public`: `int apply(int price) { ... }`. What happens?
options: It compiles and the method is package-private
It compiles but is never called
It does not compile, because interface methods are public and an implementation cannot reduce access
It compiles with a warning
explanation: Methods declared in an interface are implicitly public. An implementing method with weaker access is rejected by the compiler.

question: `checkout(int price, Discount discount)` calls `discount.apply(price)`. A new `SeasonalOff` class implements `Discount`. What must change in `checkout`?
options: Nothing, the call is resolved to SeasonalOff at run time
A new overload for SeasonalOff
An instanceof chain for each discount type
The method must become generic
explanation: The parameter has the interface type, so any implementation can be passed and the right apply runs by polymorphism. That is the reason to depend on the interface.

question: A method takes `Box<Number> box`. A caller holds a `Box<Integer>` and passes it. What is the result and the fix?
options: It compiles, because Integer is a Number
A compile error; change the parameter to Box<? extends Number> to accept it for reading
A run-time ClassCastException
A compile error; cast the argument to Box
explanation: Generic types are not covariant: Box<Integer> is not a Box<Number>. An upper-bounded wildcard accepts any Box of a Number subtype when the method only reads from it.

question: Why does `static <T> T create() { return new T(); }` not compile?
options: Methods cannot have type parameters
T must be declared as an interface
Static methods cannot create objects
T is erased at run time, so the program does not know which class to instantiate
explanation: Type arguments are removed after compilation, so the run-time code has no class to construct for T. Pass a factory object or a supplier instead.

question: You write `static <T extends Comparable<T>> T larger(T a, T b)`. Why is the bound needed to call `a.compareTo(b)`?
options: Without it, T could be any type, and not every type has compareTo
Bounds make the method faster
compareTo exists only on generic types
It stops callers from passing null
explanation: An unbounded T is treated as Object, which has no compareTo. The bound guarantees every T supports it, so the call type-checks.
